glossary.definition: Dough of nixtamalized corn. Fresh masa from a tortillería is best. For tamales ask for masa para tamal, sin preparar (unprepared), ground coarser than tortilla masa. Masa harina is the dried flour version.
Rendered pork lard. Buy it fresh and soft from a butcher shop. The shelf-stable white blocks are hydrogenated and taste flat.
A different plant from Mediterranean oregano, more citrusy and grassy. Rub it between your palms over the pot or bowl.
Mexican (Ceylon) cinnamon: soft, flaky layered bark that breaks in your fingers. Milder and sweeter than cassia.
A pungent herb for black beans, quesadillas, chilaquiles and pozole verde. There's no real substitute; leave it out if you can't find it.
A big heart-shaped leaf that tastes of anise and sassafras. Used in pozole verde, pipián and Oaxacan moles.
Dried Mexican avocado leaves, toasted before using. They add an anise note to barbacoa and black beans.
Unrefined cane sugar pressed into cones. Grate it or melt it in water. Dark brown sugar is the closest swap.
Annatto seeds ground with spices into recado rojo paste. Sold in bricks; the base of cochinita pibil.
Seville sour orange, used in the Yucatán. Swap: two parts orange juice to one part lime juice.
The large white corn for pozole. Bagged precooked maíz pozolero beats canned hominy.
A sour cactus fruit for mole de olla and salsas. Lime juice can stand in.
Queso fresco crumbles; cotija and añejo are dry and salty; Oaxaca and asadero melt and stretch; panela holds its shape when warm.
Mexican cultured cream, thinner and saltier than sour cream. Thin sour cream with a little milk if you can't find it.
Glazed clay ollas, cazuelas and jarritos for beans, coffee and atole. Buy pieces marked Sin Plomo (lead-free); old or unmarked glazes can leach lead.
A natural mineral salt from the old lakebeds of central Mexico, the traditional leavening for tamales, dissolved in water (often with tomatillo husks).
